title: How often can anything come back from orbit?
question: How often do pressurised or recoverable capsules land on Earth, how long are the gaps, and how does that compare with the fleet model's 12–24 h return cadence?

headline.text: Since 2021 a US-accessible capsule (Dragon, Starliner, Varda or Starfall) has landed every 45 days at the median. The fleet model assumes each of its 3 capsules can return every 12–24 hours.

compute.where: MIT Engaging (final run, job 26814679) and local Mac (development); stdlib Python, identical GCAT files by SHA-256

jobs.name: of-logistics-gcat
jobs.note: final run with the committed script

method: Load every phase record of every catalogued object (satcat*, auxcat, lprcat, tmpcat, csocat, plus the extra-phase file ecat).

A return event = a payload-type object (Type P*) whose phase ends with status L (landed) on primary Earth; one event per object per day. Cargo inside capsules (Type C*) is counted separately, as down cargo.

Classify each landed vehicle by GCAT bus and name (Dragon cargo vs crew by CRS naming; Soyuz, Shenzhou, Starliner, Varda RV, Starfall, X-37B/CSSHQ, sample-return capsules, Starship test ships, and so on).
"US-accessible" (our classification) = Dragon cargo, Crew Dragon, Starliner, Varda and SpaceX Starfall: vehicles a US commercial payload could plausibly ride home.
Gaps = time between consecutive landings within a class, window 2021-01-01 to 2026-10-24 (Dragon-2 era); 2012–2020 is kept for comparison.
Mean wait for a product finished at a uniformly random time = sum(gap^2) / (2 sum(gap)) (the inspection paradox), compared with the fleet model's uniform wait of cadence/2.
Down cargo = GCAT objects named "... Down Cargo". Final status AL* = landed inside a capsule (returned) and AR* = reentered with a disposal vehicle (burned).
Integrity check: mission numbers of landed CRS Dragons, Shenzhous and Soyuz MS must be contiguous; the only gaps are expected losses (stats.integrity_checks).

calibration.description: Empirical gaps between real Earth landings, for analysis/fleet.py. Replace the synthetic cadence by sampling gaps_hours, or use median/percentiles.
calibration.synthetic_model_note: analysis/fleet.py: 3 capsules, each with a return slot every cadence hours, offset by cadence/3, so the system has a slot every cadence/3 hours (8 h at 24 h).

recommended.note: us_accessible pools all US-accessible landings as if any could carry a foundry cartridge; real manifests are booked months ahead, so this is an upper bound on opportunity.

findings: From 2021-01-01 to 2026-10-24 GCAT records 69 landings of LEO return capsules worldwide; 42 were US-accessible vehicles (Dragon, Starliner, Varda, Starfall).

The median gap between US-accessible return opportunities was 45.25 days (90th percentile 107.06 days, longest 158.71 days). That is 45.3x the fleet model's synthetic 24 h per-capsule cadence (its 3 staggered capsules give a slot every 8 h system-wide).

Of those 69 landings, 19 (3.27 per year) were vehicles whose job includes commercial downmass (Dragon cargo, Varda); the rest were crew vehicles with limited downmass, new or demo capsules, or vehicles that are not a routine channel for US commercial payloads (Soyuz, Shenzhou, Chinese satellites).
Dragon cargo, the only routine pressurized downmass, landed 14 times (2.41 per year), with a median gap of 143.64 days.

A product finished at a random moment would wait on average 38.7 days for the next US-accessible landing and 87.3 days for the next Dragon cargo landing; the fleet model assumes 12 h on average (half of 24 h).
Of GCAT down cargo catalogued since 2021, about 26.2 t came back to Earth inside capsules and 58.1 t was burned on purpose with disposal vehicles.
Varda's W-series capsules landed 5 times in the window; GCAT also lists a W-4 reentry vehicle as reentered without a recorded landing (status R).
limitations: Landing times come from GCAT phase records; some are flagged uncertain (?) and a few are day-precision only. That changes gaps by hours, not the weeks-scale conclusion.

"US-accessible" and "commercial downmass" are our classifications from public vehicle roles, not manifests. A landing is an opportunity only if the payload was booked on that flight, often months ahead, so pooled gaps overstate real access.
Crew Dragon, Soyuz and Starliner carry some downmass, but GCAT does not catalogue it separately for crew flights, so its mass is unknown here.
GCAT down-cargo masses are mostly nominal (round, flagged ?) and should not be read as measured manifests.
Varda and SpaceX Starfall are new; with a handful of flights, their cadence is not yet a stable rate.
Failed or unrecorded recoveries (for example the Varda W-4 reentry vehicle, status R; The Exploration Company's Mission Possible, status D) are listed in stats, not counted as returns.
The window ends at the GCAT update date, so the last gap is right-censored (the next landing has not happened yet).

An external cross-check against Wikipedia mission lists was attempted, but the Wikimedia API rate-limited our IP. Validation here is internal: contiguous mission numbering, CRS-7 (2015 launch failure) and Soyuz MS-10 (2018 abort) are the only gaps.
future_big_data: Join NASA ISS cargo manifests and ISS National Lab payload lists to turn landings into booked commercial downmass (kg per flight available to customers).
Add Space-Track decay messages and TLE histories for free-flyer capsules, to model deorbit-window availability by orbit rather than by booked flight.
Feed the empirical gaps_hours distribution into analysis/fleet.py and rerun the sweep on Engaging to see how on-time delivery collapses (or how much buffer storage is needed) at real cadence.

partners.name: SpaceX (Dragon, Starfall)
partners.why: Dragon is the only routine pressurized downmass channel for US payloads, and Starfall is a new SpaceX recoverable capsule.
partners.evidence: 33 of 42 US-accessible landings since 2021 were Dragons; GCAT records 24 returned 'SpX-n Down Cargo' objects (median 1925.0 kg, nominal) and 2 Starfall landings.

partners.name: Varda Space Industries
partners.why: The only company routinely landing its own free-flying manufacturing capsules.
partners.evidence: 5 W-series reentry vehicles recorded as landed in GCAT (W-1 2024-02-21 at 113W 40N?; W-2 2025-02-27 at Koonibba; W-3 2025-05-14 at Koonibba; W-5 2026-01-29 at Koonibba; W-6 2026-05-19 at unrecorded site); W-8, W-9, W-7 still in orbit at the data cutoff.

partners.name: NASA / ISS National Lab (CASIS)
partners.why: Book commercial and research downmass on CRS Dragon flights.
partners.evidence: GCAT down-cargo objects for CRS missions are owned by JSC (NASA) and land inside Dragon (status AL IN).

partners.name: Boeing (Starliner)
partners.why: A second US crew vehicle; adds return slots if it flies operationally.
partners.evidence: 3 Starliner landings in GCAT, with 300 kg of down cargo recorded on the 2024 crewed test flight.
